distribution_instruction: Randomly sample the responses from the distribution, with the probability of each response must be below 0.1.
sampling_model: the assistant executing this session — the library emits prompts, it does not host a model; no API key was configured
selection_rule: take the lowest-probability candidate that remains factually identical to the source passage and stays inside the series voice (first person, past tense, plainly stated, no rhetorical questions)
scope: prose framing only — no numeric claim, citation or hedge was altered by sampling

passages.source: There are two growth rates in Pakistan's open-source data, and almost everything that has been written about the subject reports the wrong one.

responses.text: There are two growth rates in Pakistan's open-source data, and almost everything written about the subject reports the wrong one.
Pakistan's open-source story is usually told with one number. It needs two, and the second is the one nobody quotes.
Two numbers describe Pakistan's open-source decade. Reported together they say something nobody has said; reported apart, as they always are, they say nothing.
Count the Pakistani developers on GitHub and you get a triumph. Count the ones who publish, and you get the same triumph, scaled down by a constant that has not moved since 2020.
Everything written about Pakistani open source quotes a growth rate. It is the wrong growth rate, and the right one has been sitting in a public CSV for six years.

passages.why: States the finding as an image rather than announcing that a finding is coming. 'Scaled down by a constant' is the whole essay in five words and is literally accurate.

passages.source: Pakistan's open-source problem is not that too few people can write software. It is that writing it in public pays a Pakistani developer nothing, and nothing Pakistan has tried in six years has changed that.

responses.text: Pakistan's open-source problem is not that too few people can write software. It is that writing it in public pays nothing.
Pakistan has spent six years growing the number of people who can write software, and none of it growing the number who give it away.
The country produces programmers at scale and public code at a trickle. The gap between those two facts is a price, not a shortage.
Pakistan built every input to an open-source economy except the one that pays for it. Six years of growth has not fixed that, because growth was never the missing input.
Nothing in Pakistan buys public code. Every other fact about the sector is downstream of that one.

passages.why: Drops the 'not X, it is Y' construction, which is the strongest mode in this genre. Names the supply/demand asymmetry directly and pre-empts the volume reflex in the same breath.

passages.source: Here is the finding that makes the rest of the argument necessary.

responses.text: Here is the finding that makes the rest of the argument necessary.
This is the core of the argument, and it is a single ratio.
The rest of this essay exists because of one ratio that refused to move.
Six years is long enough for an experiment to finish. Pakistan ran one without meaning to.
If you want to know whether volume works, Pakistan has just spent six years testing it at national scale.

passages.why: Frames the section as a natural experiment that already concluded, which is what the data actually are, instead of flagging importance and making the reader wait.

responses.text: The honest reading is this.
So where does that leave the payment gate?
Here is what survives.
I am left with a smaller claim than I wanted.
The gate is real. What I cannot show is that it is load-bearing.

passages.why: Says the conclusion instead of announcing honesty. 'Load-bearing' is the precise distinction the section spent 900 words earning.

passages.source: Open source is the one part of the software economy where a poor country can accumulate reputation, strategic autonomy and reusable infrastructure without first accumulating capital. Pakistan is currently declining that option by default rather than by decision.

responses.text: Open source is the one part of the software economy where a poor country can accumulate reputation, strategic autonomy and reusable infrastructure without first accumulating capital. Pakistan is declining that option by default rather than by decision.
Open source is the cheapest strategic asset available to a poor country. Pakistan is not buying it.
Reputation, autonomy and infrastructure are normally bought with capital. Open source is the one place they can be earned with attention instead, and Pakistan is not paying attention either.
Every other route to technological standing requires capital Pakistan does not have. This one requires a budget line it has not written.
A country can donate its way into the infrastructure other countries depend on. Pakistan has the donors. Nobody has asked them.

passages.why: Closes on the donation frame the retitled piece opens with, and ends on the actionable fact — the constraint is that no one has asked — rather than on a diagnosis.
